title: Let AI Widen the Search. Keep the Judgment.
summary: AI is great at listing leads fast and weak at choosing which source to trust. How to split search from judgment, with an incident example and a source receipt prompt.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Checkout latency jumps right after a deploy. You paste the error rate graph, a few log lines and the diff into an AI assistant. In under a minute you have three leads: a new N+1 query in the cart service, the database connection pool hitting its limit, or a cold cache after the restart. That list would have taken you a good twenty minutes to put together. Nice.

The assistant also sounds very sure that it's the N+1 query, and nobody has opened the logs yet. That's the moment where two different jobs separate: finding the candidates, and deciding which one is true.

Search and judgment are two jobs

Search asks what might matter. Judgment asks what's supported, what's risky, what changed and what action is justified. AI is often great at the first job and needs a lot of help with the second.

Anthropic's write-up on its multi-agent research system shows both sides (June 2025, so the model names are from then). A setup with Claude Opus 4 leading several Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed a single Opus 4 agent by 90.2% on their internal research eval, and they note it did best on breadth-first questions that need many directions explored at once. That's search getting wider and faster. In the same post, the team admits that human testers noticed the early agents "consistently chose SEO-optimized content farms over authoritative but less highly-ranked sources like academic PDFs or personal blogs" (How we built our multi-agent research system). They fixed it with source-quality rules in the prompt. People had to spot the problem first, because choosing which source to trust is judgment.

Fast answers, shaky sources

The source problem shows up outside research agents too. In March 2025, the Tow Center at Columbia ran 1,600 queries across eight AI search tools, asking each to find the original news article behind a quote. Collectively, the tools gave incorrect answers to more than 60% of queries. Error rates ranged from 37% for Perplexity to 94% for Grok 3, and most tools rarely used hedges like "it appears" or "might" when they were wrong (AI Search Has a Citation Problem).

Those tools have been updated many times since, so treat the exact numbers as a snapshot of early 2025. The pattern is the useful part: a fast answer with a citation attached looks checked, even when nobody has opened the link.

Ask for a receipt

A simple habit keeps the speed and puts the judgment back with you: for every lead the AI gives you, ask for a receipt. Something like this, pasted after the first answer:

For each possible cause you listed:
1. What did you actually look at? (file, log line, doc URL)
2. What did you read there, and what did you infer?
3. What evidence would prove this cause wrong?
4. What haven't you checked yet?

The answers usually sort themselves. Some leads point at a real log line you can open. Others turn out to be "this pattern often causes this kind of symptom," which is a fine hypothesis and not yet evidence. Now you know which ones to check first.

Then you rank the sources yourself. A rough order that works for most engineering questions:

  1. Your own system: logs, metrics, traces, the code that's actually deployed.
  2. Official docs and changelogs for the exact version you run.
  3. The project's issue tracker and release notes.
  4. Writing from people who build or maintain the thing.
  5. Everything else, including well-ranked tutorials that may be years out of date.

What stays with you

Back to the checkout incident. You open the connection pool metrics and see the pool maxing out three minutes before the deploy. The N+1 lead, the one the assistant sounded surest about, can't explain that timing. A nightly batch job that started early can. The AI saved you twenty minutes of listing possibilities. The metrics made the call.

That's the part that stays human, and it's more than a final click on "approve." It's deciding which source counts as authoritative, which trade-off matters for this product, which failure mode you can live with, and whether the fix fits the codebase you'll still be maintaining next year. Those decisions need context the model doesn't have and consequences it won't carry.

Watch the pace

A fast conversation can make thin evidence feel like enough, simply because everything is moving. When the AI hands you a lead quickly, spend the time it saved on one real check: one log query, one reproduction, one source you open yourself.

Try this week

  • Next time you investigate a bug with AI, ask for the receipt prompt above after the first answer.
  • Open at least one cited source yourself before you repeat the AI's conclusion to anyone.
  • Write down which lead the AI was most confident about, and check afterwards whether it was right. A few weeks of this will tell you a lot about how far to trust that confidence.

This post is about investigations. For the broader habit of using AI without handing over the final call, read using AI without handing over your judgment.

faqs.q: What is the difference between search and judgment in AI-assisted work?
faqs.a: Search finds what might matter: possible causes, relevant files, candidate libraries. Judgment decides what is supported by evidence, what is risky and what action is justified. AI is often strong at search. Judgment needs context about your system and accountability for the outcome, so it stays with you.

faqs.q: How accurate are AI search tools at citing sources?
faqs.a: In a March 2025 test by the Tow Center at Columbia, eight AI search tools gave incorrect answers to more than 60% of 1,600 queries about news sources, with error rates from 37% to 94%, and they rarely hedged when wrong. The tools have changed since, but opening the cited source yourself is still the cheapest check.

faqs.q: What should I ask an AI after it suggests possible causes?
faqs.a: Ask for a receipt for each lead: what it actually looked at, what it read versus what it inferred, what evidence would prove the lead wrong, and what it has not checked yet. Then check the leads backed by real evidence first.

faqs.q: Which sources should I trust most during an investigation?
faqs.a: Start with your own system (logs, metrics, traces, deployed code), then official docs and changelogs for your exact version, then the project issue tracker, then writing by the maintainers. Treat everything else, including popular tutorials, as leads to verify.
